lines.text: Why does your watch flash green on your wrist?
Under the glass sit green lights, and next to them, tiny light sensors called photodiodes.
Blood is red because it reflects red light, and soaks up green.
Every heartbeat pushes more blood through your wrist, so more green gets absorbed.
Between beats, less blood, so more light bounces back to the sensor.
Flash that hundreds of times a second, and the dips become your heart rate.
While you sleep, Apple's newest watches switch to infrared, a light you can't see.
So that green flash? It's your watch counting your blood.

post.title: Why does your watch flash green?
post.caption:
Ever noticed your watch flashing green on your wrist? 👀💚 It's counting your blood.

Apple explains it on its support page: blood is red because it reflects red light and absorbs green light. Apple Watch pairs green LED lights with light-sensitive photodiodes to see how much blood flows through your wrist at any moment. When your heart beats, more blood flows and more green light is absorbed; between beats, less. By flashing its LEDs hundreds of times per second, the watch works out the beats per minute: your heart rate (its optical sensor supports 30-210 beats per minute). The sensor can also use infrared light: Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 use infrared LEDs during your sleep schedule.

Did you know it switches to infrared at night? Yes or no 👇 Send this to the friend who never takes their watch off.
